RECAP: Session 9 : Elastic Compute Instances

2. Instance Families: General purpose, compute, memory & storage optimized; GPU & accelerator families for AI/ML

Agenda for Today's Session
1. Serverless Basics: No server management; event-driven execution; Function as a Service (FaaS)
2. The Execution Model: Triggers & events; the handler contract; stateless execution; concurrency
3. Cold Starts & Warm Starts: Causes of cold start; init phase vs invoke phase; mitigation strategies
4. Limits & Constraints: Execution timeout, memory, payload size & ephemeral storage
5. BaaS & Anti-Patterns: Backend as a Service: managed databases, auth & storage; when not to use serverless: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load

slides.title: No Server Management
slides.lead: Elastic compute instances still require choosing and managing a virtual machine; serverless computing removes server management from the user, letting code run without any provisioning or capacity planning by the user

points.text: Covers Function as a Service (FaaS): code triggered by events
Also covers Backend as a Service: managed databases, auth, storage
Provider owns all server provisioning, patching and capacity
User supplies only code or configuration, never infrastructure

slides.notes: Stress that serverless is broader than a single compute service: it is any model removing server management. Note that BaaS returns later as managed databases and auth. Exam angle: define serverless versus FaaS precisely.

slides.label: Analogy: paying only for a taxi ride
slides.title: No Server Management
slides.notes: TR analogy: Like a taxi: you pay only for the ride, with no car, parking or servicing to manage. Likewise, serverless charges only for what you actually use, and there is no server to manage.

slides.title: What Disappears
slides.lead: Removing server management shifts operational work a virtual-machine user would normally own entirely onto the provider

points.text: Provider patches the operating system and runtime automatically
Capacity is allocated per invocation, not sized in advance
No idle infrastructure cost when the function is not running

slides.notes: Point to the AWS Lambda console as the real location where this shows up: it has no instance-sizing field, unlike EC2. Contrast with the instance sizing decision from the previous session. Exam angle: list the operational tasks serverless removes.

slides.title: Compute On Demand
slides.lead: A traditional server process runs continuously, waiting for requests even when idle; a serverless function stays absent until a triggering event occurs, then runs and stops

points.text: No continuously running process consumes compute between events
Execution begins only when an event source fires a trigger
Resource use and cost track actual run time, not uptime
Billing covers only execution time, not idle time; the environment may be kept briefly for reuse

slides.notes: Contrast an always-on EC2 instance with a function appearing only on trigger. Point out the table: initialization adds overhead only on the first call. Exam angle: event-driven execution versus a request-response polling loop. The Init duration column is a preview of the cold-start section: define it in one line here, and note that handler Duration varies between runs, so the Init column is what to compare.

slides.title: Function Vs Instance
slides.lead: Function as a Service (FaaS) makes a single function invocation the unit a platform schedules and bills, far finer-grained than an entire virtual machine

cells: Per instance, configured by the user

slides.notes: Point out that this granularity difference drives cost: functions bill in milliseconds, an instance bills for every second it runs, busy or idle. Exam angle: why is FaaS billing finer-grained than instance billing.

slides.title: Function Vs Instance
slides.notes: Point out that this granularity difference drives cost: functions bill in milliseconds, an instance bills for every second it runs, busy or idle. Exam angle: why is FaaS billing finer-grained than instance billing.

slides.title: Four Core Pieces
slides.lead: Beyond knowing a function runs on trigger, Lambda's execution model defines exactly how an invocation starts, runs and ends

items.title: Triggers and Events
items.text: What starts an invocation and the data it carries

items.title: Handler Contract
items.text: The fixed signature every function must implement

items.title: Stateless Execution
items.text: No data survives reliably between separate invocations

items.title: Concurrency
items.text: How many invocations run at the same time

slides.notes: Set up the four pieces as one map before going into each. Ask: which of these four decides how many copies of the function can run together? Answer: concurrency.

slides.title: Event Context Response
slides.lead: The handler contract is the fixed shape every Lambda function must follow so the platform knows how to call it and read its reply

points.text: `event`: payload carrying the trigger's data, JSON-like structure
`context`: runtime metadata: request ID, time remaining, memory limit
Return value becomes the response for synchronous calls (e.g., API Gateway)
Asynchronous triggers ignore it
The configured handler setting (for example, `file.function`) must match the code exactly

slides.notes: Walk through event, context and return value as the three parts of one fixed contract. Point out context is metadata about the run, not the input data. Exam hook: ask what context exposes versus event.

slides.label: Analogy: a service counter
slides.title: Event Context Response
slides.notes: TR analogy: Like a service counter: the visitor hands over a filled form (event), and the clerk also gets a token slip showing the token number and the time left to serve (context). The clerk's written reply (return value) is what the visitor receives back, just as Lambda passes event and context into the handler and sends its return value back as the response.

slides.title: Invocation Types Explained
slides.lead: A trigger decides which service calls the function, and the invocation type decides whether the caller waits for a result

points.text: API Gateway requests typically invoke the function synchronously
Asynchronous invocation: event is queued, caller gets acknowledgement only
Event shape varies by trigger: each service defines its own schema
Polling-based triggers batch several records into a single event

slides.notes: Separate the trigger source from the invocation type since both vary independently. Mention API Gateway as a synchronous example and S3 upload as asynchronous. Interviewers often ask which invocation type a given trigger uses.

slides.title: No Persisted State
slides.lead: Because an execution environment can be torn down and rebuilt at any point, a function cannot depend on anything it remembered from an earlier call

points.text: Local variables and temporary disk space are not guaranteed to persist
Each invocation may land in a fresh or a reused environment
Durable data belongs in an external database, cache or storage service
Idempotent handler logic protects against duplicate retried events

slides.notes: Explain statelessness as the price paid for elastic scaling, not a limitation by accident. Give the example of a counter variable resetting unexpectedly between calls. Exam hook: ask why Lambda functions should write session data externally.

slides.title: Scaling Via Environments
slides.lead: Statelessness is what lets Lambda run many invocations in parallel, each in its own isolated execution environment

points.text: A concurrency limit caps how many environments run at once
Reserved concurrency guarantees capacity for one function
Remaining capacity is shared across other functions in one pool
Exceeding the limit throttles invocations: sync calls get a 429 error, async events are retried

slides.notes: Tie concurrency back to the isolated environments just described: more concurrent events simply means more environments spun up together. Mention throttling as the failure mode of exceeding limits. Common interview question: what happens when concurrency limit is exceeded.

slides.title: Cold Vs Warm
slides.lead: A serverless platform does not keep every execution environment running forever; whether one must be built from scratch decides if an invocation is cold or warm

points.text: Cold start: a new execution environment is built before code runs
Warm start: an existing environment is reused, no setup needed
Every cold start runs two internal phases: init, then invoke
Idle environments are reclaimed after a period of inactivity

slides.notes: Frame this as the map before going into causes and phases individually. Point out that warm start skips a whole stage, not just runs faster. Exam hook: ask what decides cold vs warm for a given call.

slides.title: What Triggers Setup
slides.lead: A cold start, the delay from building a fresh execution environment, happens whenever no idle environment is available to reuse for the incoming request

points.text: First-ever invocation: no environment exists yet to reuse
Scale-out: extra concurrent requests need fresh environments
Idle reclaim: an unused environment was torn down earlier
New deployment: updated code forces a fresh environment build

slides.notes: Walk through the four causes as the reasons no warm environment was sitting ready. Everyday phrasing: nothing was 'kept on' for this request, so it had to be switched on. Exam hook: a deployment update is a cold-start trigger even under steady traffic.

slides.label: Analogy: a food stall's stove
slides.title: What Triggers Setup
slides.notes: TR analogy: Like a food stall that switches off its stove when there are no customers: when an order comes in and the stove is off, the cook must light it and heat the pan first, so that customer waits longer. If the stove is still hot from the last order, cooking starts immediately, just as a cold start happens only when no ready environment is available.

slides.title: Two Internal Phases
slides.lead: A cold start is not one delay but two stages stacked together: setting the environment up, then running the function logic inside it

cells: Download code, start the runtime, run code outside the handler
Runs the handler with the event payload

slides.notes: Point at the table while explaining that init is setup work, invoke is the actual code. Mention that the console reports the two separately, so they must not be confused. Exam hook: ask which phase a warm call skips.

slides.title: Two Internal Phases

points.text: Environment freezes after invoke completes, ready for reuse
Warm invocations skip init entirely and start at invoke
Init overhead delays the handler before it even starts running

slides.notes: Point at the table while explaining that init is setup work, invoke is the actual code. Mention that the console reports the two separately, so they must not be confused. Exam hook: ask which phase a warm call skips.

slides.title: What Carries Over
slides.lead: A warm start skips init, so anything created during init is already in memory when the handler runs

points.text: Reused: global variables, SDK clients, DB connections, files in /tmp
Best practice: initialize clients and connections outside the handler
Reuse is a performance bonus only; never rely on it for correctness

slides.title: Mitigation Strategies
slides.lead: Because init overhead adds latency before any code runs, several practices reduce how often it occurs or how costly it is

points.text: Provisioned concurrency: environments pre-initialized, billed even when idle
Smaller deployment package: less code to download at init
Fewer, lighter dependencies: runtime starts up faster
Scheduled warm-up calls: reduce idle reclaim, but not guaranteed
Faster-starting runtimes: interpreted languages init quicker than JVM-based ones

slides.notes: Explain that provisioned concurrency trades idle cost for predictable latency, unlike pure pay-per-invocation. Everyday phrasing: keeping a few shops pre-opened costs rent even with no customer. Exam hook: ask why provisioned concurrency is not free despite serverless billing being usage-based.

slides.title: Four Operational Boundaries
slides.lead: Every Function as a Service (FaaS) platform bounds how long, how much memory, how much data, and how much local disk a function may use, since unmetered execution would inflate cost indefinitely

points.text: Ephemeral storage: temporary local disk (/tmp), lost when the environment is torn down
Memory allocation: RAM assigned, with CPU scaled proportionally
Payload size: maximum request and response body size
Ephemeral storage: temporary local disk cleared after execution

slides.notes: Introduce the four limit categories before detailing each; mention the Lambda console's Configuration tab as where these are set. Interview hook: ask why serverless needs hard limits despite auto-scaling.

slides.title: Maximum Run Duration
slides.lead: A function that never finished would hold resources and billing open forever, so every invocation carries a maximum duration after which the platform forcibly stops it

points.text: AWS Lambda timeout: configurable up to 15 minutes maximum
Default timeout is 3 seconds unless explicitly raised
Timed-out invocation returns a task timed out error
Long batch or streaming jobs need a different compute model

slides.notes: Explain timeout caps cost and resource hold time, not just failures. Point to the General configuration section, where the default 3-second timeout of s10-serverless-demo can be viewed and changed. Exam hook: ask what happens to in-progress work at timeout: it is killed, not paused.

slides.label: Analogy: booked time in a gaming zone
slides.title: Maximum Run Duration
slides.notes: TR analogy: Like a game in a gaming zone that switches off when the booked time ends, even mid-level, a function is stopped at its timeout whether or not the code has finished.

slides.title: Sizing And Data Caps
slides.lead: Memory is sized separately from the instance families studied earlier, because a function's memory setting also fixes its CPU share and its cost rate

cells: CPU scales up with memory, to several vCPUs
Container images allow up to 10 GB

slides.notes: Stress that payload limits differ for synchronous versus event-driven calls, and memory also sets CPU power. Point to the memory setting under General configuration, which shows 128 MB for s10-serverless-demo. Exam hook: ask why the asynchronous payload cap is smaller than the synchronous one.

slides.title: Sizing And Cost
slides.lead: Higher memory raises per-millisecond cost, so right-sizing memory balances speed against spend, the same trade-off used when sizing compute instances
slides.notes: Stress that payload limits differ for synchronous versus event-driven calls, and memory also sets CPU power. Point to the memory setting under General configuration, which shows 128 MB for s10-serverless-demo. Exam hook: ask why the asynchronous payload cap is smaller than the synchronous one.

slides.title: Temporary Local Disk
slides.lead: A function sometimes needs scratch space mid-execution, unzipping a file or caching a lookup, so each execution environment gets a temporary disk at /tmp, wiped when that environment is removed

points.text: Default ephemeral storage is 512 MB per execution environment
Configurable up to 10,240 MB (10 GB) if needed
Data in /tmp does not persist across cold starts
Not durable: use managed databases or object storage instead

slides.notes: Clarify ephemeral storage is scratch space tied to the environment's lifecycle, not a database substitute. Point to the ephemeral storage field under Configuration, the same console area used for the practical function. Exam hook: ask what happens to /tmp data between two cold invocations: it is gone.

slides.label: Analogy: a hotel room after checkout
slides.title: Temporary Local Disk
slides.notes: TR analogy: A hotel room is cleaned out after checkout, leaving nothing for the next guest: just as an execution environment's /tmp storage is erased once that environment is recycled.

slides.title: Section Landscape
slides.lead:
Serverless computing covers more than functions
Backend as a Service (BaaS) supplies ready-made backend pieces, while certain workload shapes fit serverless poorly

points.text: Backend as a Service (BaaS): managed database, authentication and storage used directly
Anti-patterns: workload shapes where FaaS billing or limits cost more than they save
Three anti-pattern cases: long-running jobs, heavy state, steady load

slides.notes: Set up the two halves of this takeaway before going into either. Mention that BaaS removes even the function-writing step that FaaS still needs. Exam angle: distinguishing BaaS from FaaS is a common interview question.

slides.title: BaaS Defined
slides.lead: Backend as a Service (BaaS) is a managed backend component an application calls directly through an API, with no custom function code or server to run

points.text: Provider manages scaling, patching and availability of that backend piece
Covers data storage, identity checks and file storage as ready services
Billed per request or per resource used, not per function invocation

slides.notes: Contrast with FaaS: FaaS still runs an application's own code per trigger, BaaS has no custom code at all. Ask: is a managed database call BaaS or FaaS?

slides.label: Analogy: plugging into the power grid
slides.title: BaaS Defined
slides.notes: TR analogy: Plugging into the power grid instead of running a generator: a household draws electricity through a socket without owning a power station, just as an application calls a managed database, login check or file store without owning or running that backend.

slides.title: DB, Auth, Storage
slides.lead: Each BaaS category maps to a specific managed AWS service that an application calls instead of running its own database, login or file server

cells: A file server the application would run

slides.notes: Point to the real AWS console names so the mapping is concrete, not generic. Mention Cognito issues tokens, DynamoDB holds data, S3 holds files. Exam angle: naming the AWS service behind each BaaS category.

slides.title: DB, Auth, Storage
slides.lead: The common thread: each is reached by a direct API call, with no function or server standing between the application and the service
slides.notes: Point to the real AWS console names so the mapping is concrete, not generic. Mention Cognito issues tokens, DynamoDB holds data, S3 holds files. Exam angle: naming the AWS service behind each BaaS category.

slides.title: When It Fails
slides.lead:
Function as a Service bills per invocation and duration, and does not guarantee state between runs
Some workloads do not fit that model, and using serverless there costs more or fails outright

points.text: Cost mismatch: frequent or constant invocations add up to more than a fixed server price
Correctness mismatch: run-time limits and lost state between runs can break the job itself

slides.notes: Frame anti-pattern as a cost-and-fit mismatch, not a technical failure of serverless itself. Link the taxi analogy to the steady-load case. Exam angle: listing workload types unsuited to serverless is a standard interview question.

slides.label: Analogy: a daily commuter's taxi fares
slides.title: When It Fails
slides.notes: TR analogy: A daily commuter paying per taxi ride spends more than someone owning a car for the same fixed route: just as a workload invoked constantly, or needing a long single run, is billed and bounded in a way a dedicated server is not.

slides.title: Jobs, State, Load
slides.lead: Long-running jobs, heavy state and steady load each break a different assumption FaaS makes, and each has a better-fitting alternative

rows: Exceeds the function's execution timeout limit
Execution is stateless; in-memory data is not guaranteed between runs
A server holding state in memory or on disk
Per-invocation billing costs more than a reserved instance running continuously

slides.notes: Link timeout and stateless execution to what the execution-model and limits slides already defined: this is where that limit stops fitting a workload. Mention the utilisation threshold as the cost trigger an interviewer may probe.

slides.title: Jobs, State, Load
slides.lead: Reserved compute beats per-invocation pricing once load stays near continuous; the break-even point varies with memory size and run time, and 40% utilisation is only a rough guide
slides.notes: Link timeout and stateless execution to what the execution-model and limits slides already defined: this is where that limit stops fitting a workload. Mention the utilisation threshold as the cost trigger an interviewer may probe.

props.title: What Gets Built
props.lead: Creating a Lambda function, then invoking it to observe cold and warm starts

steps.text: Create the Lambda function `s10-serverless-demo` in one available region
Create a test event and invoke the function
Compare the first and third invocations: Duration and Init duration
Clean up the function, execution role and log group

props.title: Function and Handler
props.lead: The function is created with an automatically created execution role, and the Python handler is deployed
props.caption: `s10-serverless-demo` created successfully

props.title: Test Event Run
props.lead: A test event is saved and used to invoke the function once; a successful run returns `statusCode` 200
props.caption: Test event `s10-test-event` being created

props.title: Test Event Run
props.caption: Successful run: `statusCode` 200 and the handler message

props.title: Observed Summaries (1/2)
props.lead: The Init duration line appears only when a new execution environment is built before the handler runs
props.caption: First invocation: Duration 1.96 ms, Init duration 99.72 ms

props.title: Observed Summaries (2/2)
props.caption: Later invocation: Duration 40.98 ms, no Init duration line
props.note:
Cold-start cost is Init duration plus Duration, about 101.7 ms here (billed as 102 ms), against 40.98 ms for the warm run
Handler Duration alone varies between runs, so Init duration is the evidence to compare

steps.text: Expected result: `statusCode` 200, an Init duration on the first invocation, and none on a later one
A later invocation is not guaranteed to be warm, so record exactly what the console shows
Clean up: delete the function, then review the IAM execution role and the CloudWatch log group `/aws/lambda/s10-serverless-demo`
